job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Fatima Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I log on at 8:30 from my desk at Lumen Pay, a fintech start-up in Tarn City with about 40 people. I'm a junior sales operations analyst, so I clean customer data, build reports and write the first drafts of sales emails. I use AI for most of that, all day, and I check what comes out. I rent a room in a house with two other women, and my loan is 35,000. In the evenings I run a small online shop selling hand-embroidered scarves, which I started in my last year of university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, a good tool that stays a tool. At work I'd tell Joss, my manager, we should keep using it for the dull parts and keep people for the thinking and the customers. At home my family would be glad, since they never trusted the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel secure but not rich. I earn 24,200, the loan takes 180 a month, and the shop brings in about 120. A start-up can fold, so my security is only as good as the firm. In a calm world I can plan, though, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and aim to be promoted within a year. I'd put more time into the shop, maybe 400 a month by next spring, and put that against the loan. I'd keep an emergency fund of 500 in a separate account. And I'd keep going to the mosque on Fridays, which keeps me centred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Pleasantly boring. The one thing that nags is the start-up and whether it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How likely is it that Lumen Pay folds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, one in three over the next three years. We've got one big client, and Joss admits it. So even in the world where nothing changes, I'm keeping my CV fresh and the shop growing, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it folded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full time on the shop for a few months while applying to bigger firms. I'd live on savings, which are tiny, so it would be tight. But I'd rather be tight and in control than wait for a letter.

say: It's a good tool that stays a **tool**; keep people for thinking and customers.
I'd tell Joss (my manager) to use it for the **dull parts**.
think: I feel secure but not rich: 24,200 pay, **180 a month** to the loan and about 120 from the shop.
A start-up can **fold**, so my security is only as good as the firm.
do: Aim for a **promotion** within a year.
Grow the shop to about **400 a month** by next spring and put it against the loan.
Keep a **500** emergency fund in a separate account.
feel: **Calm** and pleasantly boring, with one nag about the start-up.
S0.quote: I'd rather be tight and in control than wait for a letter.
fieldNote: The real risk is her **employer**: one big client, one in three odds of folding.
Already has a **side business** that doubles as an exit.
Her **faith** keeps her centred and she says so plainly.

steps.text: Keep building reports and cleaning customer data at Lumen Pay
Grow the scarf shop to about 400 a month by spring
Keep a 500 emergency fund and put shop income against the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the kind of change that rewards people who adapt. At work I'd tell Joss we should rebuild how the sales team works around the tools, and I'd offer to lead it. With my family I'd say it's like the shift from shops to online, which my uncle's shop lived through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own job is exposed, because data cleaning and first-draft emails are on the card. But I'm the one who does it with AI already, so I could be the one running it. If the start-up shrinks, I'm in trouble. If it grows, I'm useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a short plan for how sales ops could run with half the people, and give it to Joss. I'd take a course on data analytics in the evenings. I'd use AI in the shop for product photos and listings. And I'd start putting aside an extra 100 a month, in case the start-up lays people off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, nervous, and a bit protective of the people around me. It's like being on a fast bus, I'm not sure where it's going but I'd rather be on it than at the stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A plan to run sales ops with half the people. Doesn't that cut your own colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, and I thought about that. But if I don't do it, a competitor will, and then none of us have jobs. I'd rather propose it and argue for retraining the others, than be the one who wasn't ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kiran, who does our customer calls. He's 26, he's good with people but slow with systems. I'd want to move him into the account side, where the relationships matter. I'd say it to Joss before the cuts, not after.

say: This is the kind of change that **rewards** people who adapt.
I'd offer Joss (my manager) to lead the rebuild around the **tools**.
think: My job is **exposed**, since data cleaning and first-draft emails are on the card.
I do it with AI already, so I could be the one **running** it.

Take an evening **data analytics** course and use AI for shop photos.
Put aside an extra **100 a month**.
feel: **Excited** and nervous, on a fast bus I'd rather be on than at the stop.
S1.quote: I'd rather propose it and argue for retraining the others, than be the one who wasn't ready.
fieldNote: Accepts the **conflict** of proposing cuts and pairs it with a call for retraining.

Leans on **family** history, her uncle's shop, to make sense of change.

steps.text: Write a plan to run sales ops with half the people
Take an evening data analytics course
Put aside an extra 100 a month
Use AI for scarf shop photos and listings to sell more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enormous, and families, mosques, churches and neighbours need to hold each other up. I'd say governments should help people with retraining and local work, but I'd also say each of us has to move fast. I'd say it to my team and my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the start-up won't last, and my whole field goes with it. Sales operations is analysis and writing, and the machine does those better. Debt of 35,000 and a tiny cushion make this scary. The only thing in my favour is that I already know how to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the shop and on anything that sells to real people. I'd scale it fast: more products, a stall at the weekend market in Tarn City, maybe a partnership with a boutique. I'd take a part-time job in a shop or a care home to cover rent. I'd also join my community's savings circle, where a group puts in money each month and one takes the pot. I'd talk to my uncle about a spare room if it got tough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty frightened. But I'm used to working under pressure, so I'd turn it into a to-do list. The fear shows up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shop sells to real people. Why not just trust the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a machine can make a scarf design, but customers like knowing a person made it. That's my edge, and it's a small one. Handmade and local might matter more when everything else is automatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you ask your uncle for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. He's proud, and so am I. I'd say I'd help in his shop in exchange for a room, so it's work, not charity. In our family you don't take, you swap.

say: It's **enormous**, and families, mosques and neighbours need to hold each other up.
Governments should help with retraining and **local work**, but we must move fast too.
think: The start-up won't last and **sales operations** goes with it.
With 35,000 of debt and a tiny cushion this is **scary**, though I know the tools.
do: Scale the **shop** with more products, a weekend market stall and a boutique partner.
Take a part-time job in a shop or **care home** for rent.
Join the community savings circle and ask my **uncle** about a spare room.
feel: **Frightened**, but I turn it into a to-do list and the fear shows up at night.
S2.quote: Customers like knowing a person made it.
fieldNote: Chooses **handmade** as her edge in a machine world.
Offers **work for a room** to her uncle, keeping pride intact.
Uses her community's **savings circle**, a traditional safety net.

steps.text: Scale the scarf shop with a weekend market stall in Tarn City
Take a part-time job in a shop or care home to cover rent
Work in my uncle's shop in exchange for a spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance if we use it. I'd say to my friends to learn the tools and build something of their own. I'd say the government should support small business and training, not just cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm anxious but optimistic. In five years I could have cleared half the loan, grown the shop into a proper business and moved up at a bigger firm. When AGI arrives, I'd want to be an owner rather than an employee. That's the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change jobs within a year to a more stable firm, using my experience with the tools. I'd put the shop on a real footing: a website, a small supplier network and an employee for the busy months. I'd pay the loan down 200 a month. And I'd learn a trade side of the business, like how to run a workshop, so I could expand into something physical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and tense. It's like knowing there's a storm in five years and building a good roof before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by owner rather than employee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the machines do the thinking, the people who own things get the benefits, and the people who work for them don't. I want to own a bit of something real, even if it's small. Like a workshop, a shop, or part of a firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that realistic on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly, yes. It might take the full five years and a lot of grafting. But I'd rather aim for it and fall short than not try. And my family would help with advice, even if they can't help with money.

say: Five years is a real **chance** if we use it.
The government should support **small business** and training, not just cheques.
think: I'm anxious but **optimistic**: loan half cleared, a proper shop and a stable job.
When AGI arrives I want to be an **owner** rather than an employee.
do: Change to a more **stable firm** within a year.
Put the shop on a real footing with a **website** and a small supplier network.
Pay the loan down **200 a month**.
feel: **Hopeful** and tense, like building a good roof before the storm.
S3.quote: I'd rather aim for it and fall short than not try.
fieldNote: Her answer to AGI is **ownership**, which fits her market-friendly views.
Honest that it is **slow** on her pay and might take the full five years.

steps.text: Move to a more stable fintech or finance firm within a year
Build a website and supplier network for the scarf business
Pay the student loan down by 200 a month
Learn how to run a small workshop for physical products

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and the smart move is to build skills and own something. I'd say to everyone I know that this isn't a reason to panic, it's a reason to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be in good shape. By 32 I could have the loan cleared, a small business of my own, and a family. The thing I'd watch is whether I'm building something that AGI doesn't make pointless, and I'd keep checking that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Lumen or a similar firm for three or four years, building the shop on the side. I'd clear the loan by 26, then invest part of the shop income. By 28 I'd consider the shop my main income. I'd marry within five years, and I'd want my parents close. I'd use the new tools as they arrive, since I like learning them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite good. A touch uneasy, since I know I'd want to use the time well. But mostly I'd feel lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you uneasy about using the time well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable and drift. A decade feels long until it's gone. I'd put dates on things, like a loan cleared by 26 and the shop income by 28, so I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your children anything different about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to make things and own things, and to be kind to people. And to learn the tools without worshipping them. I think that's a lesson I'd want to give any child, AGI or not.

say: Ten years is generous; build **skills** and own something.
It's not a reason to panic, it's a reason to **prepare**.
think: I'd be in good shape: loan cleared, a small **business** and a family by 32.
I'd keep checking that I'm building something AGI doesn't make **pointless**.
do: Stay at Lumen or a similar firm three or four years while building the **shop**.
Clear the loan by **26**, then invest part of the shop income.
Treat the shop as my **main income** by 28 and marry within five years.
feel: **Quite good**, a touch uneasy about using the time well, mostly lucky.
S4.quote: A decade feels long until it's gone.
fieldNote: Sets **dates** to avoid drifting, a sign of her self-discipline.
Wants her **parents** close in her future plans.
Teaches her imagined children to **make** and own things.

steps.text: Make the scarf shop my main income by 28

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Even with all the tools, two years is too short to turn my debt and my shop into something solid. What would help is small business support, community help and a bit of time, so people can build something before it hits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptive doesn't mean being safe. I use AI every day, and I know better than most how quickly it's getting good.

headlineQuote: Being adaptive doesn't mean being safe.
portrait: **Fatima** is 22, a business graduate working as a junior sales operations analyst at a start-up in Tarn City.
She owes **35,000**, has a tiny cushion and runs an online scarf shop in the evenings.
She is traditional and faithful, favours work and small **ownership** over handouts, and uses AI every day.
She builds the shop and a savings circle in the fast scenarios, and aims to be an **owner** when there's time.
Her real risk is her **employer**, since one big client holds up the start-up.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because two years is too short to turn her debt and shop into something solid.
whatWouldHelp: Small business **support**, community help and a bit of time to build something before it hits.
